It's six PM. Long day for both of you. She walked in the door fine, and then one sock seam sent her over the edge.

Here's what's actually happening. She held it together all day. School, transitions, following rules, keeping it cool. By the time she gets home, the tank is empty. The socks didn't cause the meltdown. They just broke the dam.

So instead of the lecture, you sit down next to her. You don't fix the socks. You just say, 'sounds like you're really done today.' And within about thirty seconds, she's not angry at you anymore. She's just tired.

That's the whole thing. You stopped looking for the attitude and started looking for the empty tank.

scripts.title: two pans are actually faster
scripts.summary: One pan means one temperature, and that's why your weeknight meals are taking longer than they should.
scripts.hook: Everyone says one-pan meals save time. They're actually making you slower.
scripts.body:
One pan means one temperature. So when you're searing chicken, your broccoli is sitting in the same heat, steaming instead of caramelizing. By the time the chicken's done, the broccoli's mushy. And if you lowered the heat for the broccoli, your chicken never got a real sear.

Two pans fixes both. Chicken on high, broccoli on medium. You're not babysitting either one. They finish at the same time and they both actually taste like something.

Chicken and broccoli, one pan: 22 minutes of temperature management. Two pans: you're eating in 16. The extra cleanup is literally one pan.

scripts.title: why your 20-minute recipe takes 40
scripts.summary: The dirty secret of weeknight recipe times, and the one check that fixes it.
scripts.hook: Every recipe says twenty minutes. You're still cooking at 7:45. Here's why.
scripts.body:
You get home, pull up a recipe, it says quick weeknight dinner, twenty minutes. So you start grabbing stuff. Garlic. Onion. Fresh herbs. Ten minutes later nothing's in the pan yet.

Here's what's actually happening. When a recipe says twenty minutes, it means twenty minutes of heat. Not twenty minutes from fridge to plate. The chopping, the measuring, the setup? That's invisible time. It doesn't count in their math.

So before you touch anything, skim the ingredient list and just count the chopping. Garlic, onion, herbs, that's already eight to ten minutes right there. More than five minutes of prep and you're not looking at a twenty-minute dinner. You're looking at thirty-five, minimum.

That's the number you actually plan around.

scripts.title: progressive overload is not what you think
scripts.summary: Chasing new maxes every week is the wrong move for desk workers, here's the smarter way to actually progress.
scripts.hook: Everyone tells you progressive overload means hitting a new max every week. That's completely backwards if you have a desk job.
scripts.body:
Your nervous system can only handle so much. You're already carrying stress from eight hours at a desk. Chase a new max on top of that and you're just stacking fatigue. Recovery tanks, gains flatline, and you burn out.

Here's what actually works. Pick eighty percent of your max and hit it for the same weight, same reps, every session. Week after week. Your muscles adapt, your connective tissue strengthens, and your body locks in the movement instead of fighting inflammation.

Real example. Deadlift max is four hundred pounds. You're pulling three-twenty for eight reps, three times a week. Same weight every time. After twelve weeks, three-twenty feels easy. Then you add five pounds. That's it. That's real progression.

Not chasing a PR every Friday. Not grinding through a new max when you're already running on empty. Just consistent reps at the right weight, letting your body actually adapt.

scripts.title: you don't need to know dentistry to sell
scripts.summary: Industry expertise isn't the edge in B2B sales, asking better questions about workflow pain is.

The assumption is that deep industry knowledge gives you the edge. It doesn't.

What closes deals is being able to spot exactly where their workflow breaks and costs them money. We've seen founders with zero clinical knowledge outsell people who knew the terminology, because they asked better questions. The dentist doesn't care if you know the difference between a filling and a crown. They care that their admin is spending three hours a day rebooking cancellations.

That's the thing worth knowing. Not the jargon. The pain.

So stop trying to become an industry expert before you start selling. Find someone doing the job you're selling to and ask them what their actual day looks like. The details will come. The pain shows up fast.

scripts.summary: Dental clinic feature requests sound like signal but aren't. Here's the two-question filter that actually predicts what gets used.
scripts.hook: You're in the demo. The clinic manager leans back and says, 'We'd pay more if you had this one thing.' You write it down. You feel like you cracked the code.
scripts.body:
Six months later you ship it. A full sprint. You're proud of it. Then you check the analytics and nobody's touching it. Not the clinic that asked. Not anyone.

This happened to us three times. Same pattern every time. And the thing is, they weren't lying in the demo. They just weren't telling you the truth about how they'd actually use it. What someone says they want and what they actually reach for at 2pm on a Tuesday are two completely different things.

So now I run two questions before anything goes on the roadmap. One: 'How often are you doing this today?' Two: 'Can you show me your current workaround?' If they hesitate on either one, I don't build it. The features that actually get used are the ones that kill a real, active pain. Not the nice-to-haves people think they should want.
